variants.title: Choose the grant
variants.context: Choose the grant from the client’s trust boundary: server web clients use Authorization Code with PKCE and keep tokens on the backend; SPAs and native apps are public clients using Authorization Code with PKCE; machine workloads use Client Credentials. Never ship a shared secret in browser or app code and call it confidential.
variants.prompt: A single-page app in the browser needs user-delegated access. Which design?
options: Public client using Authorization Code with PKCE, behind a backend-for-frontend.
Implicit grant, so the token arrives in the redirect fragment with no code exchange.
Client Credentials, with the client secret shipped inside the JavaScript bundle.
optionFeedback: Browsers cannot protect a shared secret, and PKCE binds the code without one.
A fragment token leaks through history and referrers, and Implicit is retired for new designs.
Anything in the bundle is readable, and Client Credentials carries no user delegation.
variants.hint: Can this client protect a secret from its users?
variants.explanation: Prefer a backend-for-frontend when durable tokens can remain off the browser.

variants.title: Choose the grant
variants.context: Choose the grant from the client’s trust boundary: server web clients use Authorization Code with PKCE and keep tokens on the backend; SPAs and native apps are public clients using Authorization Code with PKCE; machine workloads use Client Credentials. Never ship a shared secret in browser or app code and call it confidential.
variants.prompt: A nightly batch job needs to call an API as itself, with no user involved. Which grant?
options: Resource Owner Password, with the job storing a service account password.
Client Credentials as a confidential workload.
Authorization Code with PKCE, driven by a headless browser at midnight.
optionFeedback: Holding a reusable password defeats delegation and the grant is retired for new designs.
The client acts on its own behalf; no user identity or consent is created.
Authorization Code needs a resource owner at the keyboard, and this job has none.
variants.hint: Is there a resource owner in this flow?
variants.explanation: Client Credentials represents the client itself.

variants.title: Choose the grant
variants.context: Choose the grant from the client’s trust boundary: server web clients use Authorization Code with PKCE and keep tokens on the backend; SPAs and native apps are public clients using Authorization Code with PKCE; machine workloads use Client Credentials. Never ship a shared secret in browser or app code and call it confidential.
variants.prompt: A mobile app embeds a client secret in its binary and calls itself confidential. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because compilation and obfuscation hide the secret.
It should switch to the Implicit grant so no client secret is needed.
Anyone with the binary can extract the secret, so it is a public client.
optionFeedback: Compilation is not secrecy; a shipped binary can be unpacked and read.
Implicit removes the secret but returns the token in a fragment, which is worse.
Distributed code cannot keep a shared secret, so use PKCE in an external user-agent.
variants.explanation: A secret shipped to every device is public. Follow RFC 8252 patterns for native apps.

variants.title: Bind the code with PKCE
variants.context: PKCE binds a transaction-specific secret to the Authorization Code flow: create a high-entropy verifier, send its SHA-256 challenge with the S256 method, the server binds the short-lived code to client, redirect URI, and challenge, and the code is redeemed only with the original verifier.
variants.prompt: A public client starts login. Put the PKCE steps in order.

items.text: Send the SHA-256, base64url challenge with the S256 method in the authorization request.
Redeem the code with the original verifier; the server recomputes the challenge and rejects mismatches.
The server issues a short-lived, single-use code bound to client, redirect URI, and challenge.
Generate a high-entropy code verifier and keep it in client-side transaction state.

variants.hint: The verifier never appears in the authorization URL.
variants.explanation: Create → challenge → bind → prove possession. The code may cross the browser because it cannot be redeemed alone.

variants.title: Bind the code with PKCE
variants.context: PKCE binds a transaction-specific secret to the Authorization Code flow: create a high-entropy verifier, send its SHA-256 challenge with the S256 method, the server binds the short-lived code to client, redirect URI, and challenge, and the code is redeemed only with the original verifier.
variants.prompt: An attacker intercepts the authorization code. Put the steps that make it useless in order.

items.text: The challenge derived from it was bound to the code at issuance.
The client had generated a verifier only it holds.
The attacker presents the stolen code without the verifier.
The token endpoint recomputes the challenge, finds no match, and rejects the redemption.

variants.hint: PKCE does not stop theft; it stops redemption.
variants.explanation: The code is not sufficient for redemption by itself.

variants.title: Bind the code with PKCE
variants.context: PKCE binds a transaction-specific secret to the Authorization Code flow: create a high-entropy verifier, send its SHA-256 challenge with the S256 method, the server binds the short-lived code to client, redirect URI, and challenge, and the code is redeemed only with the original verifier.
variants.prompt: A confidential server client adopts PKCE. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Redeem with the verifier and the client credential at the token endpoint.
Send the S256 challenge in the front-channel request.
Generate the verifier on the backend.
Receive the code bound to the challenge.

variants.hint: RFC 9700 recommends PKCE even for confidential clients.
variants.explanation: Servers must support PKCE; public clients must use it.

variants.title: Read the rejection
variants.context: Security comes from validation at each boundary: a stolen code needs the verifier; redirect URIs are compared by exact string match; a reused refresh token signals compromise and revokes the grant family.
variants.prompt: A callback arrives at https://app.example.com/cb/ but the registered URI is https://app.example.com/cb. What should the authorization server do?
options: Accept it, since the host and the path prefix both match.
Reject before redirecting, because the match is exact.
Accept it after normalizing away the trailing slash.
optionFeedback: Host-only matching lets an attacker pick any path on the origin, including an open redirect.
Wildcards and loose matching enable token theft.
Normalizing before comparison reintroduces the looseness that exact matching exists to prevent.
variants.explanation: The native loopback port exception is narrow; nothing else is loose.

variants.title: Read the rejection
variants.context: Security comes from validation at each boundary: a stolen code needs the verifier; redirect URIs are compared by exact string match; a reused refresh token signals compromise and revokes the grant family.
variants.prompt: A refresh token that was already rotated out is presented again. What does rotation imply?
options: Issue a fresh token, since a dropped response looks the same.
Ignore the reuse and let the current refresh token keep working.
Reuse of an invalidated token signals compromise; revoke the grant family.
optionFeedback: A retry and a theft look identical here, so a new token hands an attacker a live session.
Ignoring it leaves both copies working and discards the only signal that the token leaked.
Rotation keeps the relationship between generations so reuse is detectable.
variants.hint: Why is the old token even being presented?
variants.explanation: Refresh reuse detection is a security signal, not an error to swallow.

variants.title: Read the rejection
variants.context: Security comes from validation at each boundary: a stolen code needs the verifier; redirect URIs are compared by exact string match; a reused refresh token signals compromise and revokes the grant family.
variants.prompt: Where must the access token come from on the happy path?
options: The browser URL fragment, read by the client after redirect.
The state parameter, carried back on the callback URL.
The token response, reaching only its intended resource server.
optionFeedback: A fragment puts the token in the address bar, where history and extensions can read it.
state is a CSRF check on the browser transaction, never a carrier for credentials.
Tokens in URLs leak through history and logs.
variants.explanation: The access token comes from the token response, not a browser URL.

variants.title: Separate the controls
variants.context: Redirect URI answers where the response may go; state answers which browser transaction; PKCE answers who can redeem the code. They participate in one transaction but answer different questions.
variants.prompt: Which control answers “which browser transaction does this callback belong to?”
options: PKCE, since the verifier is unique to each transaction.
The redirect URI, since only one URI is registered.
state, a one-time unpredictable value bound to the session.
optionFeedback: The verifier is per transaction but is checked at the token endpoint, not the callback.
One registered URI is reused by every transaction, so it cannot tell them apart.
Validate and invalidate state at the callback.
variants.hint: Which control is validated at the callback?
variants.explanation: Keep redirect, state, PKCE, and nonce responsibilities separate.

variants.title: Separate the controls
variants.context: Redirect URI answers where the response may go; state answers which browser transaction; PKCE answers who can redeem the code. They participate in one transaction but answer different questions.
variants.prompt: Which control answers “who can redeem this code?”
options: nonce.
PKCE.
state.
optionFeedback: nonce binds an ID token to a login request.
The verifier proves possession at the token endpoint.
state ties the transaction to a browser session.
variants.hint: Which control is checked at the token endpoint?

variants.title: Separate the controls
variants.context: Redirect URI answers where the response may go; state answers which browser transaction; PKCE answers who can redeem the code. They participate in one transaction but answer different questions.
variants.prompt: Application data is carried inside state. What must be true?
options: Carrying signed data in state removes the need for PKCE.
It must be tamper-protected and still one-time and unpredictable.
Nothing extra, because the value is opaque to the browser.
optionFeedback: PKCE answers who may redeem the code, which no amount of data in state can answer.
Carrying data does not remove the CSRF role.
Opaque is not protected; an attacker can read the value and forge a callback.
variants.hint: Does carrying data change what state must guarantee?
variants.explanation: Protect application data inside state against tampering.

variants.title: Know what OAuth proves
variants.context: An access token tells a resource server what access was granted. It is not a proof of login; use OpenID Connect for authentication. The resource server validates issuer, audience, expiry, and scope before serving.
variants.prompt: A client receives an access token and treats it as proof that the user logged in. What is wrong?
options: It should decode the access token and read the username claim.
An access token describes granted access, not a completed login.
Nothing, because the server issues the token only after a login.
optionFeedback: The token is encoded for the resource server audience, and its claims are not a login assertion.
OAuth is not a login protocol.
The user may have had a live session, so the token proves a grant, not a fresh authentication.
variants.explanation: Use OIDC when the client needs identity semantics.

variants.title: Know what OAuth proves
variants.context: An access token tells a resource server what access was granted. It is not a proof of login; use OpenID Connect for authentication. The resource server validates issuer, audience, expiry, and scope before serving.
variants.prompt: A resource server checks only that the token’s signature is valid. What else must it enforce?
options: Only the expiry, since the signature already proves origin.
Issuer, audience, expiry, scope, and its own authorization rules.
Nothing else, because only its own issuer signs the tokens it sees.
optionFeedback: Expiry blocks replay of old tokens but not a live token minted for another audience.
A valid signature is one gate among several.
One issuer signs tokens for many audiences, so signature alone accepts another service's token.
variants.hint: Which token could pass a signature check and still be wrong?
variants.explanation: The resource server enforces the token; the authorization server issues it.

variants.title: Know what OAuth proves
variants.context: An access token tells a resource server what access was granted. It is not a proof of login; use OpenID Connect for authentication. The resource server validates issuer, audience, expiry, and scope before serving.
variants.prompt: Does a Client Credentials grant create a user identity or consent?
options: Yes, the identity is the service account owner.
No, the client acts on its own behalf.
Yes, consent is recorded when the secret is issued.
optionFeedback: The workload is the principal, and no human owner is a party to this token.
No resource owner participates.
Registering a client is an administrative act, not a resource owner granting access.
variants.explanation: Machine clients act on their own behalf.
